title: Editing Fundamentals

learn.summary: Editing is the second half of photography — every great darkroom print was an edit, and Ansel Adams reworked prints for decades. The reliable order of operations: crop and straighten, then exposure, then contrast, then color, and stop before it looks "edited". Restraint distinguishes editing from decorating.

do: Edit one photo from your camera roll tonight using only four moves — crop, exposure, contrast, one color tweak — and stop there.

children.title: Edit With Intent

learn.summary: Before touching a slider, answer one question: what should this photo make someone feel, and what is blocking that? Every adjustment then serves the answer — brighten to lift, crop to remove the argument's noise, deepen shadows for weight. Sliders moved without intent converge on the same oversaturated nowhere.

do: For your next three edits, write the one-sentence intent first ("make the morning feel quiet") and delete any adjustment that does not serve it.

children.title: Crop, Exposure, Contrast

learn.summary: The big four do 90 percent of the work: crop (recompose and straighten horizons — a tilted horizon is the most common amateur tell), exposure (overall brightness), contrast (the distance between darks and lights), and highlights/shadows recovery. Master these before ever opening the effects drawer. Free tools like Snapseed or any phone's built-in editor cover all of them.

do: Take five old photos and improve each using only crop, straighten, exposure, and contrast — no filters, no saturation.

children.title: Presets vs Skills

learn.summary: Filters and presets are someone else's decisions applied blind — fine as a starting point, corrosive as a substitute for judgment. The literacy test: after applying a preset, open its settings and read what it actually changed. A photographer who understands five sliders will outgrow a library of 500 presets.

do: Apply your favorite filter to one photo, then recreate its look from scratch with manual sliders on a copy — note which adjustments it was hiding.

children.title: Ethics of Editing

learn.summary: The line runs between interpretation and deception: brightening, color grading, and cropping interpret; adding or removing objects fabricates. Photojournalism forbids fabrication outright — wire services have fired photographers for cloning out distractions — while art photography permits anything declared honestly. Know which contract each image signs with its viewer.

do: Write your own three-rule editing code this week (e.g., "never remove objects from documentary shots") and pin it in your notes app.
